---
title: "Coming from ggdag or dagitty"
description: "Map familiar ggdag and dagitty calls to metrodag, draw the adjustment sets you choose, and report the DAG."
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", error = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3, fig.align = "center",
  dev = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svglite" else "png",
  fig.ext = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svg" else "png",
  dev.args = list(bg = "white"))
library(metrodag)
has_dagitty <- requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)
```

This article is for readers who already draw DAGs with ggdag or analyse them
with dagitty. It maps familiar calls to metrodag, works through a DAG with two
minimal adjustment sets, and shows how a metrodag figure can support the
reporting of a DAG.

## What changes and why

Several ggdag functions, such as `ggdag_adjustment_set()`, analyse the graph
as they draw it. metrodag keeps drawing and analysis apart:

- **Layout and drawing are separate.** `layout_metro_dag()` computes node
  positions and arrow routes once. The layout is deterministic: the same graph
  gives the same geometry on every platform, with no seed. `metro_dag()` and
  `plot_metro_dag()` draw that geometry, so several analyses can share it.
- **Roles are annotations you supply.** Exposure, outcome, adjusted,
  unobserved and selected variables come from your arguments or from the
  statuses declared in a DAGitty graph. metrodag never infers a role from the
  graph, and roles never move a node or an arrow.
- **Plotting never checks adjustment.** metrodag does not compute adjustment
  sets, and drawing a figure never runs a dagitty check. Ask dagitty, or call
  `check_metro_adjustment()`, when you want one.
- **Text is measured on the output device.** Labels are wrapped and placed when
  the figure is drawn, at its real size, so check and export a figure at its
  final width.
- **Your graphs work as input.** `metro_dag()` accepts dagitty graphs,
  including `dagify()` results, ggdag `tidy_dagitty` objects, igraph and
  tidygraph graphs, edge matrices and `from`/`to` data frames.

## Familiar calls in metrodag

| ggdag or dagitty | metrodag |
|:----------|:------------------------------|
| `dagitty("dag { X -> Y }")` or `dagify(Y ~ X)` | Pass the graph to `metro_dag()` or `layout_metro_dag()`. Node names, isolated nodes and arrows are kept, and a `dagify()` result is read without loading ggdag. Without dagitty, a `from`/`to` data frame, or `metro_graph()` for isolated variables, describes the same graph. |
| `tidy_dagitty(dag)` | Not needed: `layout_metro_dag(dag)` computes the layout, the same every time and with no seed. A `tidy_dagitty` object is accepted too, when ggdag is installed. metrodag reads the dagitty graph inside it and the table's `label` column, but not its coordinates, and stops if the table's nodes, arrows, `status` or `adjusted` column disagree with that graph. |
| `ggdag(dag)` or `ggdag_status(dag)` | `metro_dag(dag)` draws the graph with role markers and a legend: filled markers for the exposure and outcome, squares for adjusted variables and dashed outlines for unobserved ones. |
| `exposure`, `outcome` and `latent` in `dagify()`; `[exposure]`, `[outcome]` and `[latent]` in DAGitty code | Imported as the exposure, outcome and unobserved roles. DAGitty's `[adjusted]` and `[selected]` become the adjusted and selected roles. You can also give roles to `metro_dag()`, for example `unobserved = "U"`: a role you supply replaces the imported one. Roles must not overlap. |
| `control_for(dag, "Z")` or `adjust_for()` | `metro_dag(dag, adjusted = "Z")`, or `unadjusted = TRUE` for an explicitly empty set. metrodag takes adjustment from the dagitty graph inside a ggdag object, never from its plotting table: an `adjusted` column that disagrees with that graph's `[adjusted]` nodes stops the import. |
| `ggdag_adjustment_set(dag)` | No equivalent: metrodag does not compute or suggest adjustment sets. Call `dagitty::adjustmentSets()` yourself and draw each set you choose as a view of one layout with `compare_metro_dags()`, as in the recipe below. |
| `ggdag_paths(dag)` and other path plots | `highlight_paths(p)` asks dagitty for the paths between exposure and outcome, given the plot's adjusted and selected variables, and emphasises the arrows of the open ones on the same figure. `paths = "biasing"` or `"causal"` narrows the choice, and the result's `metrodag_paths` attribute lists every path. |
| `ggdag_collider()` or `ggdag_dseparated()` | No equivalent: metrodag does not mark colliders or d-separation. Ask dagitty with `dagitty::isCollider()` or `dagitty::dseparated()`. To show the path that conditioning on a collider opens, mark it `adjusted` or `selected` and call `highlight_paths()`. |
| Coordinates from `dagify(coords = )` or `dagitty::coordinates()` | Not supported: imported coordinates are ignored, and metrodag computes its own layout. Constrain it with `direction`, `rank` (temporal order) and `align` (repeated measures on one row), and move a single label with `label_nudge`. |
| `theme_dag()` and `geom_dag_*()` layers | Not needed: metrodag draws its own layers on an empty theme. Choose `style = "publication"`, `"monochrome"` or `"metro"`, change details with `metro_style()`, and restyle single arrows with `edge_style`. `ggplot2::labs()` still adds a title or caption. |
| `ggsave("dag.pdf", width = 7, height = 5)` | `save_metro_dag("dag.pdf", p, width = "double")`. Widths are in millimetres or the presets `"single"` (85 mm), `"1.5"` (120 mm) and `"double"` (180 mm), the height is automatic, and text is measured on the export device. A figure that cannot fit every arrow and station is not written unless you pass `on_error = "warn"`; check a size first with `diagnose_metro_dag()`. `ggplot2::ggsave()` also works. |
| Labels from `dagify(labels = )` or `label(dag) <- labels` | Imported, as is the `label` column of a `tidy_dagitty` table. `labels = c(Z3 = "Shared cause")` overrides the nodes it names. Labels are wrapped and placed when the figure is drawn, clear of stations and arrows where possible; adjust them with `label_wrap` and `label_nudge`. Role arguments take node names, not labels. |
| Bidirected arcs, `X <-> Y` | Rejected unless you say how to draw them, so the assumption is never dropped silently. `bidirected = "latent"` draws each arc as an unlabelled, dashed unobserved common cause with arrows into both variables. Undirected and partially directed graphs are not supported. |

## Recipe: one view per minimal adjustment set

The bow-tie DAG below, also called the butterfly, has two minimal adjustment
sets for the total effect of `X` on `Y`. `Z3` is a common cause of `X` and
`Y`, and also a collider on the path `X <- Z1 -> Z3 <- Z2 -> Y`. Adjusting for
`Z3` closes the other back-door paths, which all pass through it, but opens
that one, which `Z1` or `Z2` then closes. Ding and Miratrix (2015) discuss the
bias this structure creates when `Z1` and `Z2` are not measured.

In ggdag, you might draw the sets like this (not run here):

```{r ggdag-sets, eval=FALSE}
library(ggdag)
bowtie_gg <- dagify(Y ~ X + Z2 + Z3, X ~ Z1 + Z3, Z3 ~ Z1 + Z2,
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y")
ggdag_adjustment_set(bowtie_gg)
```

In metrodag, the sets come from an explicit call to dagitty. Here the model is
written as DAGitty code; `metro_dag(bowtie_gg)` would read the `dagify()`
version in the same way.

```{r bowtie, eval=has_dagitty}
bowtie <- dagitty::dagitty("dag {
  X [exposure]
  Y [outcome]
  Z1 -> X; Z1 -> Z3; Z2 -> Z3; Z2 -> Y
  Z3 -> X; Z3 -> Y; X -> Y
}")
sets <- dagitty::adjustmentSets(bowtie)
sets
```

These are the minimal sets dagitty finds under the assumed graph. Compute the
layout once and give each set its own view, so that both panels share one
geometry:

```{r bowtie-sets, eval=has_dagitty, fig.height=2.8, fig.cap="Each minimal set that dagitty lists, drawn as a view of one fixed layout.", fig.alt="Two panels, Minimal set 1 and Minimal set 2, show the same drawing from left to right: Z1 at top left and Z2 at bottom left point to Z3, Z1 and Z3 point to the exposure X, and X, Z3 and Z2 point to the outcome Y. Minimal set 1 draws Z2 and Z3 as adjusted squares; Minimal set 2 draws Z1 and Z3. A shared legend lists exposure, outcome, adjusted, and observed but not adjusted."}
fixed <- layout_metro_dag(bowtie)
views <- lapply(sets, function(set) list(adjusted = set))
names(views) <- paste("Minimal set", seq_along(views))
compare_metro_dags(fixed, views)
```

The views inherit the exposure and outcome declared in the DAGitty code, and
each subtitle lists its adjustment set. Both sets meet the adjustment
criterion under this graph. Choosing between them is the analyst's decision,
on grounds the graph does not show, such as how well each variable is
measured.

## Reporting a DAG

Tennant et al. (2021) reviewed the use of DAGs in applied health research and
made eight recommendations for their reporting and use. Those that concern the
figure map onto metrodag as follows.

| Tennant et al. (2021) recommend | In metrodag |
|:----------------|:--------------------|
| 1. State the focal relationship and estimand in the study aims. | `estimand = "Total effect of X on Y"` repeats the target as the figure title. It is a label: nothing is checked. |
| 2. Make the DAG for each estimand available: in the manuscript, in supplementary material, or through a working link to a platform such as dagitty.net. | `save_metro_dag()` exports the figure for the manuscript, and dagitty's `toString()` gives the DAGitty code for a supplement, as shown below. |
| 3. Include all relevant variables, including those that were not measured directly. | Declare them `[latent]` in DAGitty code, or pass them as `unobserved`: their stations and outgoing arrows are dashed. |
| 4. Arrange the variables so that all arcs flow in the same direction, for example left to right or top to bottom. | Every metrodag layout does this: each arrow advances along `direction`, which is `"right"` by default or can be `"down"`. |
| 6. State the adjustment sets that the DAG implies for each estimand. | The set passed as `adjusted`, or declared `[adjusted]`, is listed in the subtitle and drawn as squares with an "Adjusted" legend key; `unadjusted = TRUE` reports an empty set. |
| 8. Justify any alternative adjustment set and report its estimate separately. | Draw each set as a view of one layout with `compare_metro_dags()`, as in the recipe. |

Recommendation 5 (assume, in general, that an arc exists between any two
variables) and recommendation 7 (report the estimate from the unmodified
adjustment set that the DAG implies, or its nearest approximation) concern the
model and the analysis rather than the figure; metrodag draws exactly the
arrows you supply. The recommendations do not cover selection. If a study
conditions on selection, for example by including only people admitted to
hospital, mark that variable as `selected` (DAGitty's `[selected]`). It is
drawn as a double-outlined square and listed as "Selected (conditioned on)" in
the legend.

Suppose `Z1` was not measured. Declaring it latent keeps it in the DAG, and
dagitty then finds a single minimal set. Recording the chosen set in the same
graph lets one object give the figure, the check and the supplement:

```{r report-sets, eval=has_dagitty}
reported <- bowtie
dagitty::latents(reported) <- "Z1"
dagitty::adjustmentSets(reported)
dagitty::adjustedNodes(reported) <- c("Z2", "Z3")
```

The layout depends on the graph alone, not on its statuses, so this figure has
the geometry of the recipe's panels:

```{r report-figure, eval=has_dagitty, fig.height=4, fig.cap="A figure for the manuscript: the estimand as the title, the adjustment set in the subtitle and legend, and the unmeasured Z1 dashed.", fig.alt="The bow-tie DAG drawn from left to right under the title Total effect of X on Y and the subtitle Adjusted for: Z2, Z3. Z2 and Z3 are squares; Z1 is a dashed circle whose arrows to X and Z3 are dashed. The legend lists exposure, outcome, adjusted and unobserved."}
report_plot <- metro_dag(reported, estimand = "Total effect of X on Y")
report_plot
```

Export the figure at the journal's width, and write the DAGitty code for the
supplement with dagitty's own `toString()`. Both files go to a temporary
folder here:

```{r report-files, eval=has_dagitty}
figure_dir <- tempdir()
save_metro_dag("bowtie.pdf", report_plot, path = figure_dir, width = "double")
dagitty_code <- toString(reported)
writeLines(dagitty_code, file.path(figure_dir, "bowtie-dagitty.txt"))
cat(dagitty_code)
```

The text file holds the model and the reported analysis in DAGitty's own
syntax, so a reader can reload it with `dagitty::dagitty()`.

## Using DAGitty alongside

metrodag draws the DAG; dagitty, the R interface to DAGitty (Textor et al.,
2016), analyses it. The two work together in three ways.

**In the browser.** [dagitty.net](https://www.dagitty.net/) reads the same
code: paste the code printed above into the Model code box of the web
application and choose Update DAG. Its Causal effect identification and
Testable implications panels then describe the same model, and Model > Publish
on dagitty.net puts it online, which gives the kind of link that Tennant et al.
mention.

**Testable implications.** A DAG implies conditional independencies that data
can contradict. `dagitty::impliedConditionalIndependencies()` lists them, and
`dagitty::localTests()` tests them against a data set:

```{r implications, eval=has_dagitty}
dagitty::impliedConditionalIndependencies(bowtie)
length(dagitty::impliedConditionalIndependencies(reported))
```

Each of the three involves `Z1`. In the reported graph, where `Z1` is
unobserved, dagitty lists none.

**Checks in metrodag.** `check_metro_adjustment()` passes the graph, its roles
and an adjustment set to DAGitty's adjustment criterion for a total effect.
Plotting never calls it, so call it yourself:

```{r checks, eval=has_dagitty}
check_metro_adjustment(report_plot)
check_metro_adjustment(bowtie, adjusted = "Z3")
```

Adjusting for `Z3` alone fails. `highlight_paths()` shows why: with
`paths = "biasing"`, it emphasises the open paths that are not causal, here
the one that conditioning on the collider `Z3` opens.

```{r collider-path, eval=has_dagitty, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Adjusting for Z3 alone leaves the path X <- Z1 -> Z3 <- Z2 -> Y open; its arrows are drawn thicker in red.", fig.alt="The bow-tie DAG with Z3 drawn as an adjusted square and the subtitle Adjusted for: Z3. The arrows from Z1 to X, Z1 to Z3, Z2 to Z3 and Z2 to Y are thicker and red; the arrows from Z3 to X, Z3 to Y and X to Y stay grey."}
z3_only <- metro_dag(fixed, adjusted = "Z3")
highlight_paths(z3_only, paths = "biasing")
```

A passing check concerns identification of a total effect by adjustment under
the assumed graph. It does not validate the graph, the measurements or the
estimator; see the [analysis guide](analysis-views.html#check-adjustment-separately)
for more.

## References

Ding, P., & Miratrix, L. W. (2015). To adjust or not to adjust? Sensitivity
analysis of M-bias and butterfly-bias. *Journal of Causal Inference*, 3(1),
41-57. <https://doi.org/10.1515/jci-2013-0021>

Tennant, P. W. G., Murray, E. J., Arnold, K. F., et al. (2021). Use of
directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to identify confounders in applied health
research: review and recommendations. *International Journal of
Epidemiology*, 50(2), 620-632. <https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyaa213>

Textor, J., van der Zander, B., Gilthorpe, M. S., Liśkiewicz, M., & Ellison,
G. T. H. (2016). Robust causal inference using directed acyclic graphs: the R
package 'dagitty'. *International Journal of Epidemiology*, 45(6), 1887-1894.
<https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw341>
